title: Bilkis Bano Case: Supreme Court Grants Bail to two Convicts After 17 Years in Jail, Suspends Sentence Pending Appeal
summary: Supreme Court: In an appeal arising from the conviction of persons involved in the brutal crimes committed against Bilkis Bano and her family during the 2002 Gujarat riots, a Division Bench of M.M. Sundresh and Prasanna B. Varale, JJ.

note.Facts: Convicts of the 2002 Gujarat riots, including those who gang-raped Bilkis Bano, were sentenced to life imprisonment; after more than 14 years they sought premature release and remission, which was granted by Gujarat but later challenged.
note.Issue: Whether the conviction-related sentence can be suspended and bail granted pending appeal, and which remission policy governs the convicts’ premature-release applications.
note.Held: The Supreme Court suspended the life sentences, ordered release on bail with conditions, and directed that the appeal be listed for hearing; it also held that the 9 July 1992 Gujarat remission policy governs the convicts’ cases, setting aside the later remission orders.
note.Principle: A higher court may suspend a sentence and grant bail pending appeal when incarceration is prolonged and health concerns exist, and the applicable remission policy is the one in force at the time of the offence, not a later policy.
note.Provisions: Sections 433, 433-A, 432(7) CrPC (remission); no other statutes or cases cited.
note.Exam angle: Criminal Procedure Code – remission under §§ 432-433-A and the power of higher courts to suspend sentences and grant bail pending appeal; could be asked as “issue-framing” on the applicability of the remission policy and conditions for bail/suspension.

title: Supreme Court Applies Doctrine Of Indoor Management, Says Company's Boardroom Dispute Cannot Invalidate Sale To Bona Fide Third-Party
ratio: A third-party purchaser of a company's asset relying on a Company's Board Resolution meeting to undertake the purchase is protected under the Transfer of Property…
summary: The Supreme Court has observed that a third-party purchaser of a company's asset relying on a Company's Board Resolution meeting to undertake the purchase is protected under the Transfer of Property Act, and the sale cannot be invalidated merely because there's an internal dispute regarding the authority to execute the sale deed. According to the Court, the unrelated third party cannot be expected to verify the internal affairs of the company, particularly whether the Board meeting authorising the transaction was validly convened.

note.Facts: The mother-son directors of J & A Avenues India Pvt. Ltd. disputed a board resolution dated 01-08-2015 that allegedly authorised the son to sell 9 acres 28 guntas of company land to Elaine Info Solutions Pvt. Ltd. The mother claimed she neither received notice nor participated in the meeting. The sale deed dated 04-09-2015 referred to that resolution; consideration was received and reflected in the audited accounts signed by both directors.
note.Issue: Whether a bona-fide third-party purchaser can rely on a company’s board resolution and be protected from internal irregularities of the board meeting that it could not discover.
note.Held: The Supreme Court set aside the NCLT and NCLAT decisions and held that the sale deed cannot be invalidated; the purchaser, being an unrelated third party, is protected by the doctrine of indoor management.
note.Principle: A third-party purchaser who acts in good faith may rely on a company’s apparent authority as evidenced by a board resolution; internal defects in the board’s convening or participation are not the purchaser’s burden to prove (doctrine of indoor management).
note.Provisions: Section 241 of the Companies Act, 2013 (as invoked before the NCLT); Transfer of Property Act (as the statutory basis for protection of the purchaser); the case itself (Supreme Court judgment of Justices Sanjay Kumar & Sanjeev Sachdeva).
note.Exam angle: Companies Act 2013 – Section 241 (minority oppression) and the doctrine of indoor management; could be asked to frame the issue of “what protects a bona-fide third-party purchaser against internal irregularities of a company’s board” or to list the ingredients of the indoor-management rule.

title: Supreme Court Upholds Stay On Azam Khan's Conviction In Forged Birth Certificate Case, Gives Same Relief To Wife & Son
summary: The bench dismissed the State's appeal, while allowing the appeals filed by Tazeem Fatma and Abdullah Azam Khan.

note.Facts: Azam Khan, his wife Tazeen Fatma and son Abdullah were convicted for cheating, forgery and criminal conspiracy in a forged birth-certificate case; the Allahabad High Court suspended only Azam Khan’s conviction and bail, refusing similar relief to his wife and son.
note.Issue: Whether the Supreme Court should uphold the High Court’s suspension of Azam Khan’s conviction and extend the same relief to his wife and son.
note.Held: The Supreme Court dismissed the State’s appeal, upheld the suspension of Azam Khan’s conviction and granted the same relief to his wife and son.
note.Principle: A conviction may be suspended if the appellant’s role is not materially linked to the fraudulent act; the benefit of suspension can be extended to co-accused when their involvement is similarly non-material.
note.Exam angle: Criminal Procedure Code/Criminal Law – issue of suspension of conviction and bail; could be asked on the criteria for granting suspension of conviction to co-accused under criminal law.

title: Bilkis Bano Expresses Shock Over Supreme Court Order Suspending Sentences Of Men Convicted For Gang-Rape & Murder, Says She Wasn't Heard
summary: Bilkis Bano has expressed shock and disbelief over the Supreme Court's October 28 order suspending the life sentences of two men convicted of gang-raping her and murdering members of her family during the 2002 Gujarat riots, stating that the order was passed without informing her or hearing her.

note.Facts: Bilkis Bano, a survivor of the 2002 Gujarat riots, learned from the press that the Supreme Court on 28 Oct suspended the life sentences of two convicts for her gang-rape and the murder of her family, without being called or heard.
note.Issue: Whether the Supreme Court could suspend the convicts’ sentences without informing or hearing the victim-survivor.
note.Held: The Supreme Court bench (Justices M M Sundresh & P B Varale) suspended the sentences, citing the convicts’ long incarceration, a severe handicap, and pending issues in their appeals.
note.Principle: A higher court may stay or suspend a conviction-based sentence on grounds such as prolonged imprisonment, health handicap, and pending appellate questions, even if the victim is not heard.
note.Exam angle: Criminal Procedure Code/Criminal Law – relief against conviction (suspension of sentence) and the procedural right of a victim to be heard; could be asked as “whether victim-survivor’s hearing is mandatory before a court suspends a sentence” or “ingredients for granting remission or suspension of sentence”.

title: Different States, one larger terrorist conspiracy: Supreme Court orders clubbing of J&K and Haryana criminal cases with 2025 Red Fort blast case
summary: Supreme Court: In a significant ruling on the transfer and consolidation of criminal proceedings involving an alleged larger terrorist conspiracy in connection to the 2025 Red Fort blast, arising from incidents in different States and on different dates to a common Special Court , the Division Bench of Prashant Kumar Mishra * and Shree Chandrashekhar,.

note.Facts: The Supreme Court considered three criminal proceedings – one concerning the 2025 Red Fort blast and two others from different States – alleged to be part of a larger terrorist conspiracy involving common accused, overlapping witnesses and evidence.
note.Issue: Whether the separate cases should be transferred and clubbed before a single Special Court under the NIA Act to avoid multiplicity, conflicting findings and security risks.
note.Held: The Court ordered that all three cases be transferred to and clubbed before the Special Court under the National Investigation Agency Act, 2008 at Patiala House Court, New Delhi.
note.Principle: When distinct terrorist incidents in different States are linked by a common conspiracy, common accused, and overlapping evidence, they may be clubbed and tried together in a single Special Court to prevent multiplicity of proceedings and ensure uniformity of judgment.
note.Provisions: National Investigation Agency Act, 2008; reference to State (NCT of Delhi) v. Khimji Bhai Jadeja, 2026 SCC OnLine SC 19 (distinguished).
note.Exam angle: NIA Act – question may ask to frame the issue of “clubbing of terrorist cases under the NIA Act” and to list the ingredients (common accused, overlapping evidence, risk of multiplicity) required for such consolidation.

title: ECI Failed To Produce Records Showing Unanimous Approval Of SIR Decisions: Petitioner To Supreme Court
summary: The petitioner also contended that the subsequent corrective measures taken by the ECI after the writ petition do not validate earlier decisions.

note.Facts: The petitioner alleges that the Election Commission of India (ECI) cannot demonstrate, through contemporaneous records, that decisions on the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls were taken unanimously by its three members, and that several SIR-related actions were taken unilaterally by the Chief Election Commissioner.
note.Issue: Whether the absence of contemporaneous records proving unanimity and compliance with Section 18 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 renders the SIR decisions ultra vires.
note.Held: The Supreme Court has not yet ruled on the merits; the matter is listed for hearing. The petitioner seeks production of agendas, minutes, file-notings, resolutions, electronic approvals and communications to establish whether the decisions complied with the statutory requirement of collective approval.
note.Principle: A statutory requirement of collective decision-making (Section 18, 2023 Act) must be satisfied by contemporaneous documentary evidence; mere assertions of unanimity or subsequent corrective measures do not cure a prior lack of statutory authority.
note.Exam angle: Test takers may be asked to frame an issue on “whether the ECI’s SIR decisions complied with Section 18 of the 2023 Act” or to enumerate the “ingredients of a valid collective decision under Section 18” and the evidentiary burden on a public authority to produce contemporaneous records.

title: Subsequent Amendment To Recruitment Rules Cannot Invalidate Promotion Validly Made Under Earlier Rules: HP High Court
ratio: A subsequent amendment to Recruitment and Promotion Rules prescribing additional educational qualifications cannot invalidate a promotion that was validly granted under the rules prevailing at…
summary: The High Court observed that Devi Singh had been promoted as Senior Sheristedar on November 3, 2017, in accordance with the eligibility criteria prescribed under the rules then in force. It held that the subsequent amendment dated October 16, 2024, introducing the minimum educational qualification of 10+2, could not retrospectively invalidate his existing promotion or require his demotion.

note.Facts: Devi Singh was promoted to Senior Sheristedar on 3 Nov 2017 under rules requiring only matriculation, and later to Chief Administrative Officer on 8 May 2025; a 2024 amendment introduced a 10+2 qualification.
note.Issue: Whether a later amendment to recruitment rules adding educational qualifications can invalidate a promotion made under the earlier rules.
note.Held: The amendment cannot retrospectively invalidate the promotion; the petition was dismissed.
note.Principle: A promotion validly made under the rules in force at the time of promotion remains valid despite subsequent amendments that impose higher qualifications, which apply only prospectively.
note.Provisions: Himachal Pradesh District Judiciary Staff Rules, 2022 (amended 16 Oct 2024); not stated.
note.Exam angle: Test on the applicability of amended recruitment rules (e.g., HP District Judiciary Staff Rules) – focus on prospective vs. retrospective effect of rule changes in promotion cases.

title: Calcutta High Court upholds death penalty of man for rape and murder of 5-year-old girl
summary: The Calcutta High Court on Tuesday upheld the death penalty of a man found guilty of raping and subsequently murdering his neighbour's five- year-old daughter after luring her with chocolates [ State of West Bengal v. Ashok Singh] . A Bench of Justices Arijit Banerjee and Apurba Sinha Ray noted that the convict Ashok Singh.

note.Facts: Ashok Singh lured his neighbour’s 5-year-old daughter with chocolates, raped her through vagina and anus, and killed her by striking her head; forensic DNA linked him to the victim and he was convicted of child rape, aggravated sexual assault and murder.
note.Issue: Whether the conviction and death-penalty sentence imposed by the trial court fall within the “rarest of rare” category under Indian law.
note.Held: The Calcutta High Court upheld the death-penalty, confirming the trial court’s finding that the case is “rarest of rare” and directing a three-month stay pending any Supreme Court appeal.
note.Principle: A death sentence is justified when the crime involves extreme depravity, brutality and the offender is beyond reformation, satisfying the “rarest of rare” test.
note.Exam angle: Could be asked under the Indian Penal Code (sections on rape of a child, murder) and the jurisprudence on the “rarest of rare” doctrine for death-penalty awards.
